title: 1 Thessalonians
subtitle: Turned from idols, waiting for the Son
lead: 1 Thessalonians is a short letter from Paul, Silvanus and Timothy to a church they had founded only months before in Thessalonica, the capital of Roman Macedonia, and had been forced to leave in a hurry. Most of its members had turned from the city's gods to serve "a God who lives and is true" (1:9), and they were paying for it with the anger of their neighbors. Paul writes after Timothy brings back good news: their faith and love have held. He thanks God, tells again how he lived among them, explains why he has not come back, and then teaches what they still lacked: how to live in holiness, and what to hope for when believers die.

Most scholars date the letter about AD 50, which makes it probably the oldest surviving Christian writing. It contains the New Testament's first written words about the Lord's coming (parousia), including the passage about the dead rising and the living being "caught up" to meet the Lord in the air (4:13-18), which later became the main text for the teaching called the rapture. It also contains some of Paul's harshest words about his Judean opponents (2:14-16), which later Christians turned against the Jewish people. This Plain English Translation translation follows the Greek text, and the notes give each reading fairly.
facts: Paul, writing with Silvanus (Acts' Silas) and Timothy (1:1). Almost all scholars accept that Paul wrote it.

About AD 49-51, during Paul's year and a half at Corinth (Acts 18:1-11). The anchor is the Delphi inscription, a letter of Claudius from AD 52, from which Gallio's term as proconsul of Achaia (Acts 18:12) is usually dated to about AD 51-52.
Most scholars say Corinth, after Timothy came back from Thessalonica (3:6; Acts 18:5). A note added to some manuscripts says Athens, a guess from 3:1.
The church at Thessalonica: mostly Gentile converts who had turned from idols (1:9), with some from the synagogue's circle (Acts 17:4); mostly working people (4:11).

A letter of friendship and encouragement, with a long thanksgiving (1:2-3:13), teaching on holy living (4:1-12), comfort about the dead (4:13-18), teaching on the day of the Lord (5:1-11) and short commands for church life (5:12-22).
Greek. The letter is written in the plural "we" of three senders, with Paul's "I" breaking in at 2:18, 3:5 and 5:27.
authorship: It opens "From Paul, Silvanus and Timothy" (1:1), and Paul speaks as "I, Paul" at 2:18.

Nearly all scholars, traditional and critical, hold that Paul wrote 1 Thessalonians. Its style and concerns match Romans, the Corinthian letters and Galatians, and it fits the account of Paul's journeys in Acts 17-18. In the mid-1800s a few scholars, among them Clement Schrader and F. C. Baur, doubted it; their view has found few followers (Wikipedia's article on the letter).

Some scholars, among them Walter Schmithals and others named in Wikipedia's article on the letter, have proposed complicated theories of editing and later additions in 1 and 2 Thessalonians. Most scholars read 1 Thessalonians as a single letter.

Some scholars hold that 2:13-16 was added after AD 70 (Birger Pearson, 1971); most now hold that Paul wrote it (see the chapter 2 page). A few have proposed that 5:1-11 is a later addition correcting 4:13-18; most read it as Paul's own continuation.

audience.to: The church at Thessalonica, a few months old. Thessalonica was a large port, the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia since 128 BC and a free city since 41 BC, governed by its own magistrates (Acts 17:6, 8, the politarchs) and set on the Via Egnatia, Rome's highway across the Balkans. Acts says Paul argued in the synagogue for three Sabbaths and won over some Jews, many Greeks who worshiped God and many leading women (Acts 17:1-4), and that a riot drove him out (Acts 17:5-10). The letter itself speaks to former idol worshipers (1:9) who worked with their hands (4:11), suffered from their own countrymen (2:14), and had recently lost some of their members to death (4:13). They met in houses, perhaps more than one (5:27), led by people without titles who worked among them (5:12).
audience.why: Paul had left after a short stay and could not get back (2:17-18). He feared the pressure on the converts would break their faith (3:5). When Timothy returned with good news (3:6), Paul wrote to do what he could not do in person: to thank God and strengthen them, to answer any doubt about his own motives (2:1-12), to repeat his teaching on holy living (4:1-12), to comfort them about members who had died (4:13-18), to settle their minds about the day of the Lord (5:1-11), and to make up "what is still missing in your faith" (3:10). How knowing the audience changes the reading: the letter's great passages on the Lord's coming were written to comfort new believers at a graveside, not to give a timetable of the end; and its harsh words about the Judeans were heard by Gentiles suffering from their own neighbors, a setting that later readers forgot.
views: The letter's own words (1:9; 2:14; 4:5) show a church of former idol worshipers, mostly converted outside the synagogue, perhaps in Paul's workshop.
Acts 17:4 suggests a church that began among Jews and God-fearers at the synagogue; the letter, written months later, speaks to the Gentile majority.

outline: Thanks: a church that turned from idols to the living God
How the preachers lived among them
Torn away; Timothy sent from Athens; Timothy's good news
Prayer for love and holiness at the Lord's coming
Love among brothers, and quiet work
The dead in Christ and the Lord's coming
The day of the Lord: children of the day

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads the letter against Thessalonica: a free city and provincial capital on the Via Egnatia, with its politarchs, its gods and its ruler cult, its synagogue (Acts 17), and the pressure on converts who left the city's worship; and against Paul's journey from Philippi to Athens and Corinth (Acts 16-18).

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the letter was made and when: its date about AD 50 and place among Paul's letters, its relation to Acts, proposals of partition or later additions (2:13-16; 5:1-11), the textual problems ("infants" or "gentle" at 2:7), and the development of Paul's hope for the Lord's coming.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads the shape of the letter: the long thanksgiving (1:2-3:13) closed by a prayer, the triad of faith, love and hope (1:3; 5:8), the family images (infants, nurse, father, orphan), the consolation of 4:13-18, and the contrasts of night and day in 5:1-11.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads Paul as a Jew teaching Gentiles to serve Israel's God: turning from idols, Israel's holiness laws for sexual life, the prophets' day of the LORD, Daniel's archangel and resurrection, the Dead Sea Scrolls' "sons of light"; and faces honestly the words about the Judeans in 2:14-16 and their later use against the Jewish people.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: Follows the letter in the churches: Chrysostom's homilies, Augustine and the Jesus Prayer on "pray without a break" (5:17), the debates over the rapture (4:17), the state of the dead (4:13), the gifts of the Spirit (5:19-21) and the parts of a human being (5:23).

sections.b:
Read it as a letter between friends who were torn apart. The first three chapters are mostly thanks and memories: how the converts received the message, how the preachers lived among them, how Paul tried to return and sent Timothy instead. The last two chapters are teaching, much of it a reminder ("as you know" comes again and again). The key words are given the same English each time: brothers (the whole church), the good news, coming (parousia, the Lord's arrival), anger (God's wrath), holiness, fallen asleep (died), and the day of the Lord.

Read 4:13-5:11 slowly, and remember who first heard it: a young church burying its dead.

After the greeting (1:1), a thanksgiving begins at 1:2 and keeps returning (2:13; 3:9) until the prayer of 3:11-13 closes it. That prayer names the themes of the second half: love that grows (4:9-12; 5:12-15), holiness (4:1-8; 5:23) and the Lord's coming (4:13-5:11). The letter ends with short commands, a prayer, greetings and an oath that it be read to all (5:12-28).

Acts 17:1-10 tells how the church began: three Sabbaths in the synagogue, converts among Jews, God-fearing Greeks and leading women, a riot, Jason's house stormed, and a flight by night to Berea. The letter agrees on the suffering and the hurried departure (1:6; 2:14-17), but it speaks of the readers as former idol worshipers (1:9) and implies a stay long enough for Paul to work night and day (2:9) and to receive gifts from Philippi more than once (Philippians 4:16). The two also differ on Timothy's movements (see the note at 3:1). Readers who trust Acts combine the accounts; others give the letter, as the earlier and first-hand source, the deciding voice.

No original survives. The oldest copies of parts of the letter are Papyrus 46 (about AD 200), Papyrus 65 and Papyrus 30 (both 200s; Papyrus 30 has 4:12-5:18 and 5:25-28), followed by the great codices Vaticanus and Sinaiticus (300s), Alexandrinus and Ephraemi (400s) and Claromontanus (500s). The main textual questions are at 2:7 ("infants" or "gentle") and 3:2 (Timothy as God's co-worker or God's servant); the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus, the Greek behind the KJV, add words at 1:1, 2:15, 3:13 and 5:27 and leave out a clause at 4:1. The Plain English Translation follows the SBL Greek text except at 2:7, where it follows NA28; each place has a variant entry.

2 Thessalonians has the same three senders, a nearly identical greeting and closing, and the same themes: suffering, the Lord's coming, the day of the Lord, and people who will not work. It also seems to correct a misunderstanding: that the day of the Lord had already come (2 Thessalonians 2:2). Whether Paul wrote it soon after 1 Thessalonians, or a later writer wrote it in his name, is debated (see that book).

prompts: Lamplight in a small leather-worker's shop in a Greek port city: a man with a scarred back bends over a half-sewn tent while men and women, a slave girl among them, sit on stools and sacks listening; through the open door, a street of columns and a statue of a city god. Sketched onto old rolled parchment with charcoal and ochre, mixed with cave-drawing figures and soft modern watercolor; ragged torn edges, no hard rectangular frame.
Caught up to meet the Lord

A small crowd of ancient Mediterranean people, some rising from simple graves and some standing in their work clothes, all lifting up toward a break in the clouds where a bright figure descends with a trumpet blast shown as rings of gold; drawn in the style of an early icon mixed with cave painting, on cracked parchment with fading ink washes, soft torn borders.

Dawn breaking over a sleeping city wall: on one side, figures asleep and drunk in the dark; on the other, a few people awake, wearing a breastplate and a helmet sketched in light, with the words faith, love and hope in faint Greek letters. Hand-drawn on a scroll in ochre and charcoal with modern watercolor light; soft edges, no rectangle.
reading: Abraham J. Malherbe, The Letters to the Thessalonians (Anchor Bible, 2000)
A detailed commentary that reads the letters against Greek moral teachers and the life of the young church.
John Chrysostom, Homilies on First Thessalonians
Sermons by the great preacher of Antioch and Constantinople, including his reading of the "meeting" in 4:17 as a city going out to welcome a king.
Birger A. Pearson, "1 Thessalonians 2:13-16: A Deutero-Pauline Interpolation" (Harvard Theological Review, 1971)
The fullest case that 2:13-16 was added after AD 70; read with the replies summarized on the chapter 2 page.
Frank D. Gilliard, "The Problem of the Antisemitic Comma between 1 Thessalonians 2.14 and 15" (New Testament Studies, 1989)
Argues that one comma has made Paul's words about particular Judean opponents read as a verdict on all Jews.
Jeffrey A. D. Weima, "'Peace and Security' (1 Thess 5.3)" (New Testament Studies, 2012), and Joel R. White's reply (New Testament Studies, 2013)
Two sides of the debate over whether 5:3 echoes a Roman slogan.
The Way of a Pilgrim (Russian, 19th century)
The classic Orthodox story of a wanderer who sets out to learn how to "pray without ceasing" (5:17) and finds the Jesus Prayer.
